clue.text: Rock group going downhill? (7,6)

blocks.note: the surface sells a band: musicians who play rock
read the first two words literally instead and you have lumps of stone on a slope, which can only be doing one thing

explanation.walkthrough: There is no wordplay to find — the whole clue is one picture. A group of rocks heading down a slope is doing exactly what the band's name says.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue defines the band twice over: a group who play rock, and, taken literally, the moving stones the name itself describes.

clue.text: Returning more ashen, starts to suffer extreme setback (7)

blocks.note: more ashen is PALER, written the other way round
the starting letters of both words

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a patient looking worse, which is the very world a relapse belongs to — so the definition hides in plain sight at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A relapse is a slide back into an illness or a habit you had beaten, so 'setback' names it as a reverse rather than a mere pause.

clue.text: Stage naked ramble? It's allowed (5)

blocks.note: a leg is a stage of a journey or a race
a ramble is a WALK, and a naked one has lost its outside letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Naked' is a stripping instruction: a word with its clothes off keeps only its middle. The surface is Britain's naked rambler and whether the law could touch him.
explanation.definitionFit: Legal means permitted by law, so 'allowed' is the everyday synonym — not merely tolerated but backed by the statute book.

clue.text: Popular English actor is heading directly into the wind (2,5)

blocks.note: in = fashionable, what everyone likes
Jeremy Irons, so the surname alone does the work

explanation.walkthrough: A surname standing in for its owner is a staple of the Independent. The definition sounds like weather and is in fact sailing jargon.
explanation.definitionFit: A boat in irons has stalled head to wind and will not turn either way, so the phrase belongs to sailing rather than to shackles.

clue.text: Sewers sometimes require this decongestant, ultimately, long after parties (9,6)

blocks.note: a gathering is a party, and the plural is wanted
the last letter of decongestanT
to long for something is to itch for it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sewers' here are people who sew, not drains, and anyone picturing plumbing has been caught. 'Long' is doing duty as a verb, which is where the tail of the answer hides.
explanation.definitionFit: A gathering stitch is the loose running stitch a dressmaker draws up to pull fabric into folds, so anyone making a frill genuinely needs one.

clue.text: Result in wife abandoning second shot? (4,2)

blocks.note: if a shot is a turn, the shot that comes second is turn two
W is the standard abbreviation for wife — and it is the letter that leaves

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is the setter conceding that numbering a go this way is a liberty. The surface reads as a golfer whose partner has walked off.
explanation.definitionFit: If one thing turns to another it becomes it, so 'result in' catches the outcome sense — water turning to ice is what the freezing produced.

clue.text: Ox mince we fancy in part of America (3,6)

indicators.note: anagram indicator: fancy = elaborate, dressed up differently

blocks.note: anagram fodder — nine letters to rearrange

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' sits where an adjective describing the mince would go, which is what keeps it from looking like an instruction to shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: New Mexico is one of the fifty states, so 'part of America' defines it by class — a single member named by the whole it belongs to.

clue.text: Frank is following on (7)

blocks.note: following the war, since the war — the same stretch of time
RE means on, as in a memo re expenses

explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' looks like a man's name in the surface, which is the whole disguise. RE for 'on' is a workhorse abbreviation worth banking.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone sincere says what they actually mean without pretence, which is what 'frank' describes — openness of speech rather than bare honesty.

clue.text: Scrounge from bishop prior to arrest (4)

blocks.note: B is the bishop on a chessboard
to lag someone is old slang for having them put away

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lag' is prison slang from the days of transportation — a lag is a convict — and the surface hides it behind a churchman being arrested.
explanation.definitionFit: To blag is to wheedle something out of somebody for nothing, which is what scrounging is: cadging rather than robbing.

clue.text: Blend still Champagne, say, around back of restaurant (10)

blocks.note: still = inert, going nowhere
the last letter of restauranT, which goes inside
champagne is a wine — 'say' marks it as one example

explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' is the standard flag for a definition by example. The surface is a barman's recipe, which is what lets 'still' pass as a word about the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Threads that intertwine are wound in and out of one another, and 'blend' is that idea loosened — two things merged past separating.

clue.text: God is a chicken in Spain (6)

blocks.note: the clue's own a, taken as it stands
pollo is Spanish for chicken

explanation.walkthrough: The surface accuses a deity of cowardice — 'chicken' in the English sense — while the wordplay wants the Spanish word for the bird on the menu.
explanation.definitionFit: Apollo is the Greek and Roman god of light, music and prophecy, so 'God' defines him by example, one named deity for the class.

clue.text: Renowned revolutionary has an encounter in river (8)

blocks.note: the Dee, the crossword's handiest short river — it holds the meeting
to have an encounter with somebody is to meet them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' is the instruction to turn the whole assembly round, not a Che or a Red — and that misreading is the trap the surface sets.
explanation.definitionFit: To be esteemed is to be held in high regard by other people, which is what 'renowned' says of a reputation: known, and thought well of.

clue.text: Lively American relative's dangerous illness (9)

blocks.note: pert = lively, a touch cheeky with it
US is the usual abbreviation
sis is a sister, informally

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is joinery standing for 'is', not a possessive. Pertussis is whooping cough, so the definition is not being dramatic.
explanation.definitionFit: Pertussis is the medical name for whooping cough, a bacterial infection that still kills infants, so 'dangerous illness' describes its class.

clue.text: Mistakenly enter deli with limes on either side? (4-5)

indicators.note: anagram indicator: the letters have been entered wrongly

blocks.note: anagram fodder — nine letters, in plain sight

explanation.walkthrough: Limes here are trees, not fruit — the lime avenues of an English park — and seeing that is the whole clue. The 4-5 enumeration means a hyphen.
explanation.definitionFit: A road planted with limes down both sides is tree-lined, so the definition works by example, limes being one particular kind of tree.

clue.text: Beginning to document setter's fall (4)

blocks.note: the first letter of Document
the setter speaks as I, so 'setter's' contracts to I've

explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' is the person who wrote the puzzle, so it means I — a first-person trick that recurs constantly and is worth learning early.
explanation.definitionFit: To dive is to drop suddenly and steeply — prices dive, a goalkeeper dives — so 'fall' is a plain synonym for the plunge.

clue.text: Failed to take down broadcast (4)

blocks.note: down in the sense of gloomy is BLUE

explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' is the sound signal here rather than anything to do with television, and 'down' wants the mood, not the direction.
explanation.definitionFit: If you blew your chance you failed to take it — the slang sense of squandering an opportunity, nothing to do with air.

clue.text: Source of energy from Isle of Man fish stocks (7)

blocks.note: a bass is a fish, and it takes the island inside
IOM is the usual short form of the Isle of Man

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stocks' is the container word — the old wooden frame that held a prisoner fast — while the surface offers the fish stocks a trawlerman worries about.
explanation.definitionFit: Biomass is organic matter burned or fermented for fuel, so 'source of energy' names it by what it is used for rather than what it is.

clue.text: A drink date that leads to conflict (9)

blocks.note: the clue's own opening A
gin is the crossword's default drink
to court someone is the old-fashioned way of dating them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Date' wants the verb, not the diary entry. The surface promises a night out and delivers a battlefield in Picardy in 1415.
explanation.definitionFit: Agincourt was Henry V's victory over the French, so 'conflict' defines it by example — one named battle standing for the general word.

clue.text: Book anaesthetists (7)

definitions.note: The first definition is a title, so a singular 'book' is right even though the word looks plural; the second definition is a genuine plural.

blocks.note: the fourth book of the Old Testament, after Leviticus
split the word after the fourth letter and you have people who make you numb

explanation.walkthrough: Two words, no letters to assemble. One is straight out of the Pentateuch; the other is a joke about how the answer divides.
explanation.definitionFit: Numbers is the fourth book of the Pentateuch, and an anaesthetist is literally one who numbs — the same letters read as numb-er rather than as a figure.

clue.text: Drug Republican from Rome, possibly, ignoring American (7)

blocks.note: R is the party's letter in American politics
somebody from Rome is an Italian — 'possibly' concedes it is one example among many
A for American, and it is the letter that is ignored

explanation.walkthrough: Both political words are abbreviations in disguise: one arrives as a letter, the other leaves as one, and neither means what the surface implies.
explanation.definitionFit: Ritalin is the trade name of methylphenidate, prescribed for attention deficit disorder, so 'drug' names the brand by its class.

clue.text: Blimey! Arsenal regularly making bloomer (6)

blocks.note: cor is the exclamation blimey usually follows
the regular letters of aRsEnAl

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a fan groaning at a howler, which is the other sense of 'bloomer'. Here the word wants a plant that does the blooming.
explanation.definitionFit: Correa is an Australian evergreen shrub that flowers through the winter, so 'bloomer' means something that blooms, not the blunder on offer.

clue.text: Supporter on football pitch to attempt a record most initially ignored (8)

blocks.note: a go is an attempt
the clue's own a
an LP is a long-playing record
MOST with its own initial letter ignored

explanation.walkthrough: LP for 'record' is worth banking — the long-playing vinyl album. The surface pretends to be somebody chasing a record on the pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: A goalpost is one of the uprights holding the net up, so 'supporter' is meant literally, a thing that props something rather than a fan.

clue.text: Tiny amphibian belonging to me picked up (6)

blocks.note: the amphibian is a NEWT and it belongs to ME, so 'my newt' — which run together is the answer

explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' means overheard, not lifted. The join is where the trick lives: two words of wordplay collapse into one word of answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Minute here is the adjective, stressed my-NEWT, meaning extremely small — a different word from the sixty-second one the spelling suggests.

clue.text: Hearts blocking French football club's corner (5)

blocks.note: Nice, the Ligue 1 side from the Riviera
H is hearts on a bridge scorecard

explanation.walkthrough: Hearts is a Scottish football club as well, which is the misdirection — here the word wants the card suit, and only its letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A niche is a recess set into a wall, the sheltered nook where a statue stands, so 'corner' is meant as a snug spot rather than an angle.

clue.text: Dicky learnt duet in cleaner's (10)

indicators.note: anagram indicator: dicky is British for shaky or unsound

blocks.note: anagram fodder — ten letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dicky' means unsound — a dicky heart, a dicky knee — and here it is the shuffling instruction wearing a man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A launderette is the coin-operated shop where clothes get washed, so 'cleaner's' names it by the trade, the possessive standing for premises.

clue.text: Local man keeps cool (4)

blocks.note: loCAL Man, running across the gap between the words

explanation.walkthrough: 'Keeps' is the concealment word — what keeps a thing holds it inside — and the answer straddles two words rather than sitting inside one.
explanation.definitionFit: To be calm is to stay unruffled under pressure, which is exactly 'cool' in the sense of composure rather than of temperature.

clue.text: Old tyrant uses handmaid's pants (6,7)

indicators.note: anagram indicator: pants is British slang for rubbish

blocks.note: anagram fodder — thirteen letters, apostrophe and all

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' means rubbish in modern British slang, and rubbished letters are letters out of order. The Handmaid's Tale in the surface is fine misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: Saddam Hussein ruled Iraq for twenty-four years until his overthrow in 2003, so 'old tyrant' points at one dictator, long gone, by description.
